tldr: This study extends a pretrained video diffusion model to jointly predict high-precision actions and future 3D world states by log-normalizing depth information into a unified representation, without requiring dedicated 3D encoders.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of SA-WAM. Alongside robot proprioception, actions, and multi-view RGB, log-normalized depth images are directly injected into the latent sequence of a pretrained video generation backbone (DiT) via the same frozen VAE tokenizer.
overview:
In autonomous robot policy learning, World Action Models (WAMs) that jointly predict future visual transitions and actions are attracting significant interest. They allow policies to directly inherit rich visual and physical dynamics priors learned by video diffusion models pretrained on web-scale video data. However, conventional WAMs operate almost exclusively on RGB observations and fail to leverage 3D spatial geometric information such as precise object distances and shapes.

To address this gap, the authors propose a Spatially Aware World Action Model, called SA-WAM. The core insight is a nonlinear log-scale normalization that maps metric depth data—which is naturally unbounded on the positive real line—into the bounded input domain expected by an existing frozen visual VAE tokenizer. This design avoids adding dedicated 3D encoders that could disrupt the pretrained model's balance, allowing RGB and depth images to be jointly processed as the same latent token sequence within a Diffusion Transformer (DiT).

The authors evaluate SA-WAM on the RoboCasa kitchen manipulation simulator, the LIBERO-Plus robustness benchmark, and real-world tabletop experiments with a UR5 robotic arm. With only 50 demonstrations per task, SA-WAM achieves state-of-the-art performance, significantly outperforming existing VLAs and WAMs. Furthermore, the authors show that the model's predicted future 3D geometric error strongly correlates with task rollout success, demonstrating that the world model's internal prediction quality directly links to control performance.
contributions: Proposed SA-WAM, which incorporates explicit 3D depth information into the latent sequence of a video diffusion model to handle geometric information without dedicated 3D encoders.

Developed a nonlinear log-scale normalization method that maps unbounded depth values into the input domain of a frozen VAE while preserving near-field resolution, quantitatively showing its superiority.
Achieved state-of-the-art performance on RoboCasa and the perturbation benchmark LIBERO-Plus using remarkably few demonstrations, outperforming conventional VLAs and WAMs.
Demonstrated high robustness and success rates in real-world UR5 arm tabletop manipulation experiments, even under randomized environments and misleading distractors.

Discovered that the geometric error in predicted future 3D object positions strongly correlates with rollout success (ROC-AUC around 0.88), highlighting its potential as a metric for failure diagnosis.

sections.heading: Can we teach video models depth perception alongside actions?
sections.summary: While video generation models excel at modeling physical interactions and temporal changes compared to static image-based models, conventional WAMs have been restricted to RGB observations. This paper introduces SA-WAM, which adapts depth data to a video tokenizer to jointly model 3D spatial geometry and actions within a single diffusion backbone.
sections.details:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, which integrate vision, language, and action, are gaining attention as foundational frameworks for robots to operate intelligently across diverse environments. However, many VLA models build upon Vision-Language Models (VLMs) pretrained on static images and text, leaving persistent challenges in modeling the passage of time and physical motion.

To overcome this, World Action Models (WAMs) that leverage video diffusion models trained on internet-scale video to learn physical dynamics have recently taken the spotlight. By jointly predicting future observation frames and robot actions within the same generative model, policies can directly use future visual foresight to guide control.

Yet existing WAMs rely solely on RGB images, missing 3D spatial depth and precise object geometry. In fine manipulation (such as grasping or tool handling), differences of a few millimeters or centimeters determine success or failure. While dedicated 3D policy research using point clouds has proven the importance of 3D information, naturally integrating it into generative models like WAMs has remained an open challenge.

This paper introduces SA-WAM (Spatially Aware World Action Model), which injects depth information directly into the latent frame sequence of a pretrained video Diffusion Transformer (DiT). The primary hurdle is that real-world metric depth spans from zero to infinity, whereas video VAE encoders are trained on bounded image ranges like [-1, 1]. The authors address this by introducing a nonlinear log-scale normalization that preserves high near-field resolution while compressing far-field regions. This allows SA-WAM to reuse existing powerful video tokenizers as-is without training dedicated 3D encoders from scratch, successfully instilling 3D geometric awareness into the model.

sections.heading: The intersection of video world models and 3D robot control
sections.summary: The paper contextualizes video-based world models for robot action learning alongside policies utilizing explicit 3D point clouds and depth information. SA-WAM builds on recent approaches that reuse pretrained video latent spaces for robotics, extending them to handle 3D geometry within a single unified architecture.
sections.details:
Related work spans three main research directions.

### World Models for Robot Policy Learning
While predicting future states has a long history in model-based reinforcement learning, recent research actively leverages generative video models as action priors. Approaches include generating future video before inferring actions via inverse dynamics (e.g., UniPi, Dreamitate) or conditioning action prediction heads on video latents (e.g., Mimic-Video). More recently, WAMs and Unified World Models (VideoPolicy, UWM, DreamZero, Cosmos-Policy) have unified video generation and action prediction into a single generative architecture trained end-to-end. Cosmos-Policy, in particular, cleverly substitutes parts of the video diffusion token sequence with action and proprioception tokens, yet these models remain strictly RGB-dependent.

### 3D-Aware Robot Policies
Recognizing the importance of geometry in manipulation, many methods operate directly on 3D data. Examples include point-cloud-based policies like PolarNet and PointVLA, 3D generative world models like 3D-VLA, and PointMapPolicy, which formats dense 3D coordinates as images. SA-WAM shares a similar philosophy with PointMapPolicy by handling dense depth images through existing 2D vision tokenizers, but innovates by extending this concept to a video-based WAM.

### Geometric Depth Encoding for Pretrained Vision Models
In generative modeling of depth images (such as DMD and DepthFM), nonlinear parameterizations like log-scales are widely used to efficiently represent wide distance ranges. SA-WAM adapts this insight to robotic world modeling, smoothly matching the depth ranges of wrist and external cameras to a frozen VAE.

sections.heading: Decoding depth with a frozen tokenizer: The power of nonlinear encoding
sections.summary: RGB and depth images from wrist and external cameras are tokenized into latents using the same frozen VAE and fed into a DiT alongside robot state and action tokens. Unbounded metric depths are clipped using camera-specific statistics, log-normalized to maintain near-field resolution, replicated into 3-channel images, and trained jointly under a single diffusion objective.
sections.details:
SA-WAM is built on top of a pretrained video Diffusion Transformer (DiT). The system configuration and processing pipeline are structured as follows:

### III-A Injecting 3D Modalities into World Action Modeling
The robot is equipped with three cameras ($\mathcal{V}=\{w, l, r\}$): a wrist camera and left and right external cameras. At each timestep $t$, an RGB image $I_t^c$ and metric depth $d_t^c$ are captured. A frozen video VAE encoder $E$ converts these observations into latent features. In addition to RGB latent frames $v_t^c = E(I_t^c)$, geometric latent frames $g_t^c = E(I_{d,t}^c)$ are produced from depth images converted into a tokenizer-compatible 3-channel format $I_{d,t}^c$.

The conditioning context $\mathcal{C}_t$ for the model consists of language instruction $\ell$, current robot proprioception (joint and wrist states) $q_t$, and RGB and depth latent frames $\{v_t^c, g_t^c\}$ across all viewpoints. Conditioned on $\mathcal{C}_t$, the model jointly predicts future action chunks $a_t$ and future latent observation frames $\{v_{t+H}^c, g_{t+H}^c\}$ at prediction horizon $H$ via denoising diffusion. Without any separate prediction heads, all modalities are unified simply by arranging their token positions in the sequence.

### Depth Injection and Normalization
The primary technical challenge is mapping positive real-valued metric depth $d_t^c$ into the $[-1, 1]$ range expected by the VAE without distortion. First, the 2nd percentile $d_{\min}^c$ and 98th percentile $d_{\max}^c$ are computed from each camera's training data to clip outliers. Then, a monotonic normalization function $f(z; a, b) \in [0, 1]$ is applied, scaled to $[-1, 1]$, and replicated across three channels.

The paper evaluates three normalization functions:
- Linear normalization: Uniformly scales the entire depth range, with constant sensitivity $|\partial f/\partial z|$.
- Inverse depth normalization: Transforms via $1/z$, with sensitivity proportional to $1/z^2$, heavily concentrating resolution at ultra-close distances.
- Log-scale normalization: Transforms via $\log(z)$, with sensitivity proportional to $1/z$, keeping near-field resolution high while preserving mid-to-far range accuracy.

### III-B Training Objective
The backbone uses the DiT from Cosmos-Predict2 (2B parameters), a video model tailored for physical AI, paired with Wan2.1's spatiotemporal VAE as a fully frozen tokenizer. The training target $x_0$ consists of the action chunk, future RGB latents, and future depth latents. Gaussian noise is added, and the network is trained using a single mean-squared error loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{EDM}}$ based on the Elucidated Diffusion Model (EDM) formulation. Elegantly, no modality-specific loss weight tuning is required for joint generation.

captions.F2: Detailed architecture of SA-WAM. Conditioned on observations at time $t$ (language, robot state, and RGB/depth frames from each viewpoint), a single DiT jointly denoises and predicts action chunk $a_t$, future RGB $v_{t+H}$, and future depth $g_{t+H}$ at time $t+H$.

sections.heading: Reaching SOTA with only 50 demonstrations: The geometric advantage
sections.summary: Evaluations on the RoboCasa kitchen benchmark and LIBERO-Plus perturbation benchmark show that SA-WAM achieves a 76.6% success rate on RoboCasa with just 50 demonstrations per task, substantially outperforming prior baselines. Furthermore, higher future 3D prediction accuracy strongly correlates with improved rollout success rates.
sections.details:
### IV-A Experimental Setup
Evaluations were conducted on RoboCasa (24 complex daily kitchen tasks using a Franka Panda arm) and LIBERO-Plus, which introduces perturbations across seven axes (layout, viewpoint, initial state, language, lighting, texture, and sensor noise). On RoboCasa, models were trained under the challenging regime of only 50 demonstrations per task, with average success rates evaluated across three random seeds. The DiT was trained on 40 NVIDIA H100 GPUs with batch sizes between 800 and 960.

### IV-B Ablation on Depth Normalization
The authors compared linear, inverse, and log-scale normalizations across eight representative RoboCasa tasks. In round-trip VAE encode-decode reconstruction error (AbsRel), linear normalization degraded significantly to 6.68% at close range (<0.3m), while inverse normalization collapsed at far distances with 13.19% error. In contrast, log-scale normalization achieved the lowest overall error at 0.63%, remaining stable across all distances for the wrist camera. In policy performance, log-scale normalization outperformed linear by 5.2 percentage points and inverse by 2.2 percentage points, perfectly mirroring reconstruction fidelity.

### IV-C Comparison with SOTA
Across 24 RoboCasa tasks, SA-WAM achieved a 76.6% average success rate, setting a new SOTA over existing competitive models. Compared against its base model Cosmos-Policy (67.1%) under identical demonstration counts, it achieved a 9.5-point boost. Gains were especially pronounced in tasks requiring precise 3D alignment, such as Pick-and-Place (+16.7 points) and Turn/Toggle (+11.2 points). In zero-shot evaluation under perturbations on LIBERO-Plus, SA-WAM achieved 86.6%, demonstrating superior robustness over strong VLA baselines like $\pi_{0.5}$ (84.6%) and Cosmos-Policy (81.4%).

### IV-D World Model Prediction Quality
Incorporating geometry also enhanced future RGB prediction quality. SA-WAM outperformed Cosmos-Policy across PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS metrics. Improvements were particularly prominent on wrist camera views featuring rapid motion, as well as in masked evaluations focused on robot and object regions. Grounding the model in 3D geometry helps prevent visual future predictions from hallucinating.

### IV-E Correlation Between Prediction Quality and Rollout Success
The authors measured the discrepancy between the model's predicted future 3D object position and its actual simulator position over a short horizon right after grasping. Successful rollouts exhibited small prediction errors, whereas failures showed large divergences. By setting a threshold on this 3D prediction error, 80% of failures could be detected with a false-alarm rate of only 13% (ROC-AUC around 0.88), revealing that the world model's internal foresight clearly reflects its execution success.

captions.F3: Comparison of predictions and execution on a RoboCasa pick-and-place task. In Cosmos-Policy (top), the future prediction diverges from simulator execution, leading to a grasp failure. SA-WAM (middle/bottom) accurately predicts both future RGB and depth, executing a successful grasp.

sections.heading: Validation on a real UR5 arm: Unshaken in cluttered real-world scenes
sections.summary: Tabletop manipulation experiments were conducted on a physical UR5 robotic arm using a fixed RGB-D camera. In randomized environments with distractors and texture variations, SA-WAM maintained a 77.5% completion rate, significantly outperforming baseline models that were misled by visually similar objects.
sections.details:
Beyond simulation, SA-WAM was thoroughly evaluated on a physical robotic setup.

### Experimental Setup
The setup featured a 6-DoF UR5 arm equipped with an RG6 parallel gripper and an Orbbec Femto Mega fixed RGB-D camera viewing the workspace. The action space used 8-dimensional end-effector (EE) target waypoints—consisting of absolute position, orientation (quaternions), and gripper openness—rather than high-frequency joint commands. The test suite included multi-step tabletop tasks: placing items on plates, placing items into boxes, hanging mugs, and stacking cups. Models were trained on only 20 demonstrations per task.

### Real-World Results and Robustness
Evaluations covered two settings: a "Clean" environment where only placements varied, and a "Randomized" environment featuring visually similar distractor objects and visual clutter. SA-WAM was benchmarked against Cosmos-Policy and the advanced VLA model $\pi_0$.

In the Clean setting, SA-WAM achieved an overall completion rate of 90.0% (versus 75.0% for Cosmos-Policy and 21.3% for $\pi_0$). In the more challenging Randomized setting, Cosmos-Policy dropped to 48.8% and $\pi_0$ fell to 11.3%, while SA-WAM maintained a high success rate of 77.5%.

Qualitative observations revealed that RGB-only models frequently failed by attempting to grasp dummy cups or fruits that shared similar colors and shapes. In contrast, SA-WAM leveraged depth cues to resolve precise 3D spatial relationships, grasping the intended targets without hesitation despite cluttered visual distractors.

captions.F6: Comparison in a randomized real-world setup with the UR5 arm. When visually similar distractors are introduced, Cosmos-Policy is misled by visual similarities and grasps the wrong item, whereas SA-WAM relies on depth information to correctly identify the target and complete the task.

sections.heading: Summary and outlook: A step toward true physical understanding
sections.summary: SA-WAM shows that explicit 3D geometric information can be naturally integrated into video diffusion models via log-scale normalization. While it demonstrates high sample efficiency and disturbance robustness, challenges remain regarding real-time robot deployment, such as physical alignment between predictions and actions and inference latency.
sections.details:
This study presented SA-WAM, a Spatially Aware World Action Model that incorporates explicit 3D depth information into the latent sequence of a pretrained video Diffusion Transformer. By introducing log-scale normalization, the framework reuses an existing frozen video VAE tokenizer without needing dedicated 3D encoders, enabling accurate processing of geometric signals.

Consequently, SA-WAM established new SOTA benchmarks on RoboCasa and LIBERO-Plus with high sample efficiency, using just 50 demonstrations per task. Real-world experiments on a UR5 robot arm further proved its resilience against visual clutter and distractors. Introducing geometry also enhanced visual future prediction fidelity, and future geometric errors proved to be an effective diagnostic metric for task failure.

Nonetheless, the authors outline several limitations and future research directions:
- Physical inconsistencies or mismatches can still occur between predicted future scenes and actual executed actions.
- Learning schemes or verification mechanisms enforcing strict geometric consistency are needed.
- The iterative sampling process inherent to diffusion models incurs inference latency, necessitating further acceleration and compression for high-frequency real-time closed-loop control.

takeaways: When injecting depth (3D information) into video foundation models, applying log-scale normalization through an existing frozen image VAE is simpler and more robust than adding dedicated 3D encoders.
Providing world models with 3D geometric information significantly boosts the prediction accuracy of future RGB imagery in addition to action forecasting.
Measuring the discrepancy between the model's predicted future 3D object position and actual motion allows accurate self-detection of rollout failures (ROC-AUC around 0.88).
In physical environments containing visually similar distractors, depth information resolves visual ambiguities and substantially improves resilience to domain randomization.
limitations: Because future states and actions are jointly generated via a diffusion model, iterative denoising incurs high inference latency, limiting direct application to ultra-high-frequency closed-loop control.
Physically inconsistent predictions or visual hallucinations between predicted future scenes and output actions are not completely eliminated.

The model relies on depth camera hardware specifications and valid measurement ranges, requiring additional consideration for areas where depth estimation degrades, such as transparent or specular reflective surfaces.
